source_text: Satis mihi quidem videor probasse de falsa et vera divinitate, cum demonstravi, quemadmodum probatio consistat, non modo disputationibus nec argumentationibus, sed ipsorum etiam testimoniis, quos deos creditis, ut nihil jam ad hanc caussam sit retractandum. Quoniam tamen Romani nominis proprie mentio occurrit, non omittam congressionem, quam provocat illa praesumptio dicentium Romanos pro merito religiositatis diligentissimae in tantum sublimitatis elatos, ut orbem occuparint, et adeo deos esse, ut praeter caeteros floreant, qui illis officium praeter caeteros faciant. Scilicet ista merces Romanis a diis pro gratia expensa est, Sterculius, et Mutunus, et Larentina provexit imperium. Peregrinos enim deos non putem extraneae genti magis fautum voluisse quam suae, et patrium solum, in quo nati, adulti, nobilitati, sepultique sunt, transfretanis dedisse. Viderit Cybele, si urbem romanam ut memoriam Trojani generis adamavit, vernaculi sui scilicet adversus Achivorum arma protecti, si ad ultores transire prospexit, quos sciebat Graeciam Phrygiae debellatricem subacturos. Itaque majestatis suae in urbem collatae grande documentum nostrae etiam aetati proposuit, cum Marco Aurelio apud Sirmium reipublicae exempto, die decimo sexto Kalendarum Aprilium, Archigallus ille sanctissimus, die nono Kalend. earumdem, quo sanguinem impurum, lacertos quoque castrando libabat, pro salute imperatoris Marci jam intercepti solita aeque imperia mandavit. O nuntios tardos, o somniculosa diplomata, quorum vitio excessum imperatoris non ante Cybele cognovit, ne deam talem riderent Christiani. Sed non statim et Jupiter Cretam suam Romanis fascibus concuti sineret, oblitus antrum illud Idaeum, et aera Corybantia, et jucundissimum illic nutricis suae odorem. Nonne omni Capitolio tumulum illum suum praeposuisset, ut ea potius orbi terra praecelleret, quae cineres Jovis texit? Vellet Juno Punicam urbem posthabita Samo dilectam ab Aeneadarum utique genere deleri? Quod si Hic illius arma, Hic currus fuit, hoc regnum dea gentibus esse, Si qua fata sinant, jam tum tenditque fovetque. Misera illa conjux Jovis et soror adversus fata non valuit plane: Fato stat Jupiter ipse. Nec tantum tamen honoris Romani dicaverunt fatis dedentibus sibi Carthaginem adversus destinatum votumque Junonis, quantum prostitutissimae lupae Larentinae. Plures deos vestros regnasse certum est. Igitur si conferendi imperii tenent potestatem, cum ipsi regnarent, a quibus acceperant eam gratiam? quem coluerat Saturnus et Jupiter? aliquem opinor Sterculium [sed Romae postea], cum indigenis suis. Etiam si qui non regnarunt, tamen regnabatur ab aliis nondum cultoribus suis, ut qui nondum dii habebantur. Ergo aliorum est regnum dare, quia regnabatur multo ante quam isti dii inciderentur. Sed quam vanum est fastigium Romani nominis religiositatis meritis deputare, cum post imperium sive adhuc regnum [auctis jam rebus] religio profecerit. Nam etsi a Numa concepta est curiositas superstitiosa, nondum tamen aut simulacris aut templis res divina apud Romanos constabat; frugi religio et pauperes ritus, et nulla capitolia certantia coelo, sed temeraria de cespite altaria, et vasa adhuc Samia, et nidor ex illis, et Deus ipse nusquam. Nondum enim tunc ingenia Graecorum atque Tuscorum fingendis simulacris urbem inundaverant. Ergo non ante religiosi Romani, quam magni; ideoque non ob hoc magni, quia religiosi. Atqui quomodo ob religionem magni, quibus magnitudo de irreligiositate provenit? Ni fallor enim, omne regnum vel imperium bellis quaeritur et victoriis propagatur. Porro bella et victoriae captis et eversis plurimum urbibus constant. Id negotium sine deorum injuria non est. Eaedem strages moenium et templorum, pares caedes civium et sacerdotum, nec dissimiles rapinae sacrarum divitiarum et profanarum. Tot igitur sacrilegia Romanorum, quot trophaea; tot de diis, quot de gentibus triumphi; tot manubiae, quot manent adhuc simulacra captivorum deorum. Et ab hostibus ergo suis sustinent adorari, et illis imperium sine fine decernunt, quorum magis injurias quam adulationes remunerasse debuerant. Sed qui nihil sentiunt, tam impune laeduntur, quam frustra coluntur. Certe non potest fidei convenire, ut religionis meritis excrevisse videantur, qui, ut suggessimus, religionem aut laedendo creverunt, aut crescendo laeserunt. Etiam illi, quorum regna conflata sunt in imperii Romani summam, cum ea amitterent, sine religionibus non fuerunt.
pass_a_gloss: It seems to me that I have sufficiently proved about false and true divinity, when I demonstrated, in what way the proof consists, not only in disputations and arguments, but also in the testimonies of those whom you believe to be gods, so that nothing may now be withdrawn from this cause. Since, however, the mention of the Roman name properly occurs, I will not omit the confrontation, which that presumption provokes, saying that the Romans, on account of the merit of diligent religiosity, have been elevated to such sublimity that they have occupied the world, and that they are gods, so that, beyond the others, they flourish, who perform a service to them beyond the others. Certainly, this reward was expended by the gods to the Romans for a favor, Sterculius, and Mutunus, and Larentina have advanced the empire. For I do not think that foreign gods would have wished to favor a foreign nation more than their own, and to have given the native soil, in which they were born, grew up, became noble, and were buried, to those who cross over. Let Cybele see, if she loved the Roman city as a memory of the Trojan race, certainly her own people, protected against the arms of the Achaeans, if she looked to pass over to the avengers, whom she knew would subdue Greece, the conqueror of Phrygia. And so, a great document of her majesty, bestowed upon the city, she proposed also to our age, when Marcus Aurelius, having been taken away from the republic at Sirmium, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, that most holy Archigallus, on the ninth day before the Kalends of the same month, on which he was libating impure blood, and also castrating, gave the usual commands for the salvation of Emperor Marcus, now intercepted. O slow messengers, o sleepy diplomas, by whose fault the emperor's passing was not known before, so that Cybele would not be ridiculed by Christians, for on the ninth day before the Kalends, he gave the commands, not knowing that the emperor had already been taken away. But Jupiter would not immediately allow his Cretan land to be shaken by the Roman rods, having forgotten that Idaean cave, and the Corybantic bronze, and the most pleasant odor of his nurse there. Would he not have preferred that tomb of his to the whole Capitol, so that the earth would rather excel in that, which covers the ashes of Jupiter? Would Juno have wished the Punic city, having put aside Samos, to be destroyed, beloved by the race of the Aeneadae? What if this were the armor, this the chariot of that one, this the kingdom of the goddess among the nations, if the fates allow, already then she was striving and fostering. That wretched wife of Jupiter and sister was not able to prevail against the fates: Jupiter himself is established by fate. Nor, however, did they devote so much honor to the Roman fate, giving Carthage to themselves against the destined vow and desire of Juno, as to the most prostituted she-wolf Larentina. It is certain that many of your gods have reigned. Therefore, if they hold the power of conferring empire, from whom did they receive that grace, when they themselves reigned? Whom did Saturnus and Jupiter worship? Some, I think, Sterculius, but later in Rome, with their own indigenous people. Even if some did not reign, nevertheless, they were ruled by others, who were not yet their worshipers, so that they were not yet considered gods. Therefore, it belongs to others to give empire, because empire was ruled much before these gods were encountered. But how vain is the pride of the Roman name, to attribute it to the merits of religiosity, when after the empire, or even the kingdom, religion has progressed. For even if the curiosity of superstition was conceived from Numa, nevertheless, the divine thing was not yet established among the Romans, either by statues or by temples; the religion was frugal, and the rites were poor, and there were no capitolias competing with the sky, but reckless altars from turf, and still Samian vessels, and the smell from them, and God himself was nowhere. For not yet had the talents of the Greeks and the Tuscans flooded the city with fabricated statues. Therefore, the Romans were not religious before they were great; and therefore, they were not great because they were religious. But how can they be great on account of religion, to whom greatness comes from irreligiosity? For, unless I am mistaken, every kingdom or empire is sought by wars and propagated by victories. Furthermore, wars and victories consist of the capture and destruction of many cities. This business is not without the injury of the gods. The same destruction of walls and temples, the same slaughter of citizens and priests, and not dissimilar plundering of sacred and profane riches. So many, therefore, are the sacrileges of the Romans, as there are trophies; so many are the triumphs over the gods, as over the nations; so many are the spoils, as there are still remaining statues of captive gods. And they sustain being worshiped by their enemies, and they decree empire without end to those, whose injuries they ought to have avenged rather than flattered. But those who feel nothing are injured as impunity, as they are worshiped in vain. Certainly, it cannot be consistent with faith, that they seem to have grown by the merits of religion, who, as we have suggested, either grew by injuring religion, or injured by growing. Also, those, whose kingdoms have been gathered into the sum of the Roman empire, when they lost them, were not without religions.

pass_b_english: I have, I think, sufficiently proved the difference between false and true divinity. My demonstration showed that the proof rests not only on debates and arguments, but on the testimony of the very beings you call gods, leaving nothing further to contest in this matter. Since the Roman name has now come properly into view, I will not dodge the challenge raised by the presumption that Rome owes its world dominion to the merit of its meticulous religiosity—and that the gods flourish above all others precisely because Romans serve them above all others. That would be the gods’ reward to Rome for a favor paid: Sterculius, Mutunus, and Larentina advanced the empire. I refuse to believe foreign gods would favor a foreign nation over their own, handing over the native soil where they were born, raised, ennobled, and buried to outsiders. Consider Cybele: if she loved Rome as a memorial of the Trojan race, she was protecting her own people against Achaean arms; if she looked to the avengers, she knew they would subdue Greece, Phrygia’s conqueror. She has given our own age a striking proof of the majesty she bestowed on the city. When Marcus Aurelius was cut off from the republic at Sirmium on March 17, the most holy Archigallus, on March 24—the very day he was libating impure blood and castrating himself—issued the usual commands for the emperor’s salvation, though Marcus was already dead. What slow messengers, what sleepy dispatches, whose delay kept the emperor’s passing from Cybele until after the rites, lest Christians mock such a deity! Yet Jupiter would not have let his Cretan land be shaken by Roman rods, forgetting the Idaean cave, the Corybantic bronze, and the sweet scent of his nurse there. Would he not have preferred his own tomb to the whole Capitol, so that the earth might excel in the spot covering Jupiter’s ashes? Would Juno, setting aside Samos, have wanted the Punic city destroyed—beloved as it was by the race of Aeneas? "Here are her arms, here her chariot, here her kingdom among the nations, if the fates allow; even now she strives and fosters it." That wretched wife and sister of Jupiter could not prevail against fate: Jupiter himself is established by fate. Nor did the fates, granting Carthage to Rome against Juno’s destined vow, bestow as much honor on Rome as on the utterly prostituted she-wolf Larentina. It is certain that many of your gods have reigned. If they hold the power to confer empire, from whom did they receive that grace while they themselves reigned? Whom did Saturn and Jupiter worship? Some Sterculius, I suppose—but later, in Rome, with their own indigenous people. Even those who never reigned were ruled by others who were not yet their worshipers, so that they were not yet considered gods. Therefore, the power to give empire belongs to others, because empire existed long before these gods came on the scene. How empty is the boast of the Roman name, to ascribe its greatness to religious merit, when religion only progressed after empire—or even after the kingdom—had grown. Superstitious curiosity may have been conceived under Numa, yet the divine was still not established among Romans by statues or temples; religion was frugal, rites poor, no Capitols competing with the sky, only reckless turf altars, Samian vessels, the smell from them, and God himself nowhere. The talents of Greeks and Tuscans had not yet flooded the city with fabricated statues. So Romans were not religious before they were great; therefore they were not great because they were religious. How could they be great on account of religion, when their greatness sprang from irreligion? Unless I am mistaken, every kingdom or empire is sought by wars and spread by victories, and wars and victories consist in capturing and destroying countless cities—a business not without injury to the gods. The same demolition of walls and temples, the same slaughter of citizens and priests, the same plundering of sacred and profane wealth. The Romans’ sacrileges match their trophies; their triumphs over gods equal their triumphs over nations; their spoils match the surviving statues of captive gods. And so these gods endure worship from their enemies, and decree endless empire to those whose injuries they should have avenged rather than flattered. But beings who feel nothing are injured with impunity, just as they are worshiped in vain. It simply cannot square with good faith to claim they grew by religious merits when, as we have shown, they either grew by injuring religion or injured religion by growing. Even those whose kingdoms were absorbed into the Roman sum were not without religions when they lost them.

review.notes: Pass A fails to translate the specific date provided in the Latin text, instead providing a vague description of the event. The Latin specifies 'die decimo sexto Kalendarum Aprilium' (the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April) and 'die nono Kalend. earumdem' (the ninth day before the Kalends of the same month). Pass A translates the first as 'on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April' but then fails to provide a specific date for the second instance, merely saying 'on the ninth day before the Kalends of the same month'. While Pass B correctly interprets these as March 17 and March 24, Pass A's handling of the second date is incomplete compared to the Latin 'die nono Kalend. earumdem'. More critically, Pass A contains a significant error in the clause 'non ante Cybele cognovit', translating it as 'the emperor's passing was not known before, so that Cybele would not be ridiculed by Christians, for on the ninth day before the Kalends, he gave the commands, not knowing that the emperor had already been taken away.' This is a garbled reconstruction of the Latin 'quorum vitio excessum imperatoris non ante Cybele cognovit, ne deam talem riderent Christiani.' The Latin says the delay in knowing of the emperor's death (excessum) was such that Cybele would not be ridiculed by Christians. Pass A adds a massive explanatory clause 'for on the ninth day... he gave the commands, not knowing...' which is not in the Latin text at that locus; it is an attempt to merge two sentences, but it misrepresents the syntax and the causal link of the original.
reasons: Pass A fails the fidelity test by adding an extensive explanatory clause to 'quorum vitio excessum imperatoris non ante Cybele cognovit, ne deam talem riderent Christiani' that is not present in the source, effectively hallucinating a connection between the date of the commands and the reason for the delay to satisfy a narrative logic not explicitly structured that way in the Latin. Specifically, Pass A says: 'by whose fault the emperor's passing was not known before, so that Cybele would not be ridiculed by Christians, for on the ninth day before the Kalends, he gave the commands, not knowing that the emperor had already been taken away.' The Latin does not contain the 'for on the ninth day...' clause within that specific sentence structure; it is a separate sentence/thought in the source.
